unit.label: Things & places
unit.title: A little world around you.
unit.description: 13 new words and forms. Point, describe, and say where things are.

lessons.title: This and that
lessons.subtitle: Point to someone, near or far

steps.prompt: Fill the measure-word slot in “this person”: 這 __ 人
steps.explanation: 這個人 = this person. The full pointing pattern is 這 + measure word + noun.

lessons.title: What is this?
lessons.subtitle: Ask about something. Meet your first book.

steps.prompt: You want to know what something is, not ask a yes/no question. Choose the question.
steps.explanation: 什麼 asks for the missing information. 這是書嗎？ only asks whether it is a book. Do not add 嗎 to the 什麼 question.
書 is shū: book or books. Listen for its first tone.

lessons.title: One book, two books
lessons.subtitle: A new measure word, a familiar pattern

steps.prompt: Which character means “measure word for books”?
steps.explanation: 本 (běn) means measure word for books.

steps.prompt: Fill the measure-word slot in “two books”: 兩 __ 書
steps.explanation: Books use 本: 兩本書. Keep 個 for people and students in this unit.
兩 means two before a measure word. People take 個: 兩個人.

steps.prompt: What does 這本書不大 tell you?
steps.explanation: 不大 denies big. It does not necessarily mean small, and it does not deny that the object is a book.
大 is dà, big, with a falling fourth tone. 小 (xiǎo) means small.

lessons.title: Here and there
lessons.subtitle: Say where someone or something is

steps.prompt: 你的書在那裡嗎？ Your book is not there. Choose the short answer.
steps.explanation: This is a 在 location question, so answer 不在 (no, it is not there). 沒有 answers a 有 question; 不是 answers a 是 question.

steps.prompt: In 我們都在這裡, who does 都 include?
steps.explanation: 都 refers to the group before it: 我們. The sentence says all of us are here, not everyone in the world.

steps.prompt: Choose the measure words for “one book” and “one person”, in that order.
steps.explanation: 一本書 uses 本 for books. 一個人 uses 個 for people. Choose the measure word to match the noun.
都 is dōu in this unit: all, or both for a group of two.

newVocabulary.note: Points to something nearby. Use a measure word before a noun: 這個人.
Points to something farther away: 那個人.
One question word written with two characters. 麼 has a light neutral tone.
An everyday noun to practice counting, ownership, and location.
一本書 = one book. 這本書 = this book.
兩本書 = two books. 兩個人 = two people.

newVocabulary.meaning: very; neutral link before an adjective
newVocabulary.note: In a plain description, 很 often does not strongly emphasize very.
Place it before the location. No 是 is needed: 我在這裡.
A place word made from 這 and 裡. Learn it as a whole word.
The matching place word for somewhere farther away.
Goes after the group and before the verb: 我們都在這裡.

這.note: 這 points to something nearby: this. Put 個 before 人 when naming this person: 這個人. You will practice the pattern next.
這.memory: The speech-shaped block sits inside a long walking component. Watch the order: the inner block comes first.

parts.label: 辶
parts.name: walking component
parts.description: 辶 wraps around the left and bottom. In this Taiwan form it has four strokes, written after 言. Its usual movement association does not literally explain this.

parts.label: 言
parts.name: speech-shaped block
parts.description: 言 means speech on its own. Here, recognize its seven-stroke shape without treating speech as the meaning of 這.

那.note: 那 points to something farther away: that. Compare 這個人 (this person) and 那個人 (that person).
那.memory: Four strokes on the left, then a narrow three-stroke shape on the right.

parts.label: left
parts.name: four-stroke left side
parts.description: Watch the long turn, two short horizontals, and final falling stroke. This shape helps you remember the writing, not a literal meaning equation.

parts.label: 阝
parts.name: right-side 阝
parts.description: On the right, 阝 is a form of 邑, a city or settlement component. This does not explain the modern meaning that. You will see it again in 都.

什.note: Learn 什 together with 麼: 什麼 (shénme) means what. In this word, 什 is pronounced shén.
什.memory: A person component next to a simple cross.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person
parts.description: The same two-stroke person component you met in 你 and 他. It does not make 什麼 mean a person.

parts.label: 十
parts.name: 十 · shí
parts.description: 十 is a historical phonetic component. Its sound shí is not the same as shén in 什麼, so learn the complete word’s pronunciation.

麼.note: 麼 is light-toned me in 什麼. The two characters form one question word: what. 麼 is not used by itself for what here.
麼.memory: A large upper frame over a small, three-stroke lower shape. Take the upper strokes slowly.

parts.label: 麻
parts.name: 麻-shaped upper part
parts.description: The upper eleven strokes form 麻. Use the broad top and the two tree-like groups underneath as visual landmarks; they do not explain the meaning what.

parts.label: 幺
parts.name: 幺 · small lower shape
parts.description: 幺 is the three-stroke shape at the bottom. Keep it centered beneath the large upper part.

書.note: 書 means book or books, depending on context. As with 學生, you do not need a plural ending. We will introduce its measure word before counting books.
書.memory: A tall brush-shaped top over a broad lower block.

parts.label: 聿
parts.name: writing brush shape
parts.description: 聿 is associated with a writing brush. That connection is useful for remembering a character used for books and writing.

parts.label: 曰
parts.name: 曰-shaped lower block
parts.description: The lower four strokes form a wide 曰 shape. Recognize its proportions and stroke order instead of making a literal meaning story.

本.note: 本 is the measure word used with books: 一本書 = one book. It has other meanings, including root or origin; here we practice its counting use.
本.memory: Write 木, then add a short horizontal mark near the bottom.

parts.label: 木
parts.name: tree shape
parts.description: The first four strokes form 木 (tree). The extra mark near the base helps distinguish 本 from 木.

parts.label: 一
parts.name: short lower mark
parts.description: The final horizontal marks the lower part of the tree shape. Learn the book-counting use as the pattern 一本書, not as a literal sum of tree and one.

兩.note: Use 兩 before a measure word when counting two things: 兩個人 (two people), 兩本書 (two books).
兩.memory: Find the frame and central line, then the two small paired shapes inside.

parts.label: frame
parts.name: frame and central line
parts.description: The first four strokes make the top, outer frame, and central vertical. Watch these before adding the paired shapes.

parts.label: pair
parts.name: two inner shapes
parts.description: The last four strokes form two small 入-shaped groups, one on each side. Their pairing is a useful memory aid for two.

很.note: 很 can mean very. In a simple description it often just links the subject to an adjective, without emphasizing very. You will use it with big and small.
很.memory: Three narrow strokes on the left and a six-stroke shape on the right.

parts.label: 彳
parts.name: three-stroke step component
parts.description: 彳 is often associated with steps or movement. It has three strokes, unlike the two-stroke person component 亻. Here it does not give the modern meaning very.

parts.label: 艮
parts.name: 艮 · gèn
parts.description: 艮 is the phonetic component. Its modern sound gèn is only a rough historical clue to hěn, not an exact pronunciation rule.

大.note: 大 describes size: big or large. A basic description uses 很大, without 是 before the adjective.
大.memory: Picture a person stretching both arms out wide. This is a memory aid for the shape.

parts.label: 大
parts.name: one whole shape
parts.description: A horizontal stroke crosses the two spreading strokes. Learn the three strokes together as one basic character.

小.note: 小 is the opposite of 大: small rather than big. 不大 means not big; it does not necessarily mean small.
小.memory: A central hook with a short stroke on either side.

parts.label: 小
parts.name: one whole shape
parts.description: Write the central stroke first, then the left stroke, then the right dot. Learn the shape as a whole.

在.note: 在 says where someone or something is. Put a place after it. It serves as the verb in these location sentences, so do not put 是 before it.
在.memory: Three upper strokes lead into a small 土 shape below.

parts.label: upper
parts.name: upper three strokes
parts.description: Follow the horizontal, falling stroke, and vertical shown by the guide. Recognize this upper group without inventing a modern meaning for each stroke.

parts.label: 土
parts.name: earth · 土
parts.description: The lower three strokes form 土 (earth or ground), a familiar component to notice in this character about location.

裡.note: Learn the place words 這裡 (zhèlǐ, here) and 那裡 (nàlǐ, there). 裡 can mean inside in other combinations, but these two words name places.
裡.memory: Five clothing strokes on the left, and a balanced 里 shape on the right.

parts.label: 衤
parts.name: clothing component
parts.description: 衤 is a side form of 衣 (clothing). Notice its five strokes; it is not the four-stroke component 礻. This spelling 裡 is standard in Taiwan.

parts.label: 里
parts.name: 里 · lǐ
parts.description: 里 is pronounced lǐ, the same sound and tone as 裡. It is a useful phonetic clue here.

都.note: 都 means all, or both for a group of two. Put it after the group and before the verb. In this use, it is pronounced dōu.
都.memory: An eight-stroke left side beside the same narrow right side as 那.

parts.label: 者
parts.name: 者-shaped left side
parts.description: The left eight strokes form 者. Recognize the upper crossing strokes and the 日-shaped block below; learn dōu with the whole character.

parts.label: 阝
parts.name: right-side 阝
parts.description: This is the same three-stroke component as in 那. It is a form of 邑 (city or settlement), but it does not explain the meaning all in this use of 都.

u3-point.title: Point to this or that
u3-point.pattern: 這 / 那 + measure word + noun
u3-point.explanation: 這 means this, nearby; 那 means that, farther away. When naming this person or that student, put the measure word 個 between 這 or 那 and the noun. This is the same 個 you used when counting people. 這 and 那 can also stand alone as this and that.
u3-point.remember: Use 這個人, not 這人, in the full beginner pattern here. To make a sentence, the whole phrase 這個人 can be the subject before 是.

u3-what.title: Ask what something is
u3-what.pattern: 這 / 那 + 是 + 什麼？
u3-what.explanation: 什麼 is one word meaning what. Keep it in the position of the information you want: 這是書 (this is a book) becomes 這是什麼 (what is this). Do not move what to the front as English does. 書 means book or books; the noun itself does not change.
u3-what.remember: An information question with 什麼 does not need 嗎. 那是書嗎？ asks is that a book? and expects yes or no. 這 stands alone in 這是書, so no measure word is needed between 這 and 是.

u3-books.title: A measure word for books
u3-books.pattern: number + 本 + 書 / 這 or 那 + 本 + 書
u3-books.explanation: You already know number + measure word + noun. For books, use 本 in the measure-word slot: 一本書 means one book. Use 本 with 這 and 那 too: 這本書 means this book; 那本書 means that book. The noun tells you which measure word fits.
u3-books.remember: Use 本 for books here, and 個 for people or students. 一 sounds yì before a first, second, or third tone, so 一本 is yì běn. Before a fourth tone it sounds yí, as in 一個 (yí ge). Alone, it is yī.

u3-two.title: Two books, two people
u3-two.explanation: Use 兩 for two before a measure word when counting things or people: 兩本書 (two books), 兩個人 (two people). Keep the same measure word you would use for one. No plural ending is added to 書 or 人.
u3-two.remember: Mandarin also has 二 (èr), used when counting aloud or reading digits. We will practice that later; use 兩 before 本 and 個 here. In 兩本, the first third tone changes in speech, just like 你好; the pinyin keeps dictionary tones.

u3-adjectives.title: Describe something as big or small
u3-adjectives.explanation: 大 means big and 小 means small. A simple positive description uses 很 before the adjective: 這本書很大. Do not insert 是: an adjective can do the describing without it. 很 can mean very, but in a neutral description like this it often just links the subject to the adjective, without strong emphasis.
u3-adjectives.remember: Compare an identity, 這是書 (this is a book), with a description, 這本書很大 (this book is big). Do not translate every English is as 是.

u3-not-size.title: Say it is not big
u3-not-size.explanation: For a simple negative description, put 不 directly before the adjective. 這本書不大 means this book is not big. You do not need 是 or 很 in this pattern. 不大 does not automatically mean small; it only denies that something is big.
u3-not-size.remember: 不 sounds bú before the fourth tone of 大, but stays bù before 小. This is the same tone rule you met in 不是.

u3-location.title: Say where someone or something is
u3-location.explanation: 在 means be at or in a place here. 這裡 means here, and 那裡 means there: learn each as a whole place word. 我在這裡 means I am here. Put the person or thing first, then 在, then the place. 在 is already the verb in this pattern; no 是 is needed.
u3-location.remember: 有 introduces something that exists: 有一本書 (there is a book). 在 gives the location of something: 這本書在這裡 (this book is here). 裡 is the Traditional form used in our Taiwan writing practice.

u3-location-question.title: Is it here?
u3-location-question.pattern: person or thing + 在 + place + 嗎？
u3-location-question.explanation: Reuse your yes/no question rule: add 嗎 to a location statement without changing the word order. To answer briefly, repeat 在 for yes, or 不在 for no. 在 takes 不 for a negative, unlike 有, which takes 沒.

examples.pinyin: nǐ de shū zài nàlǐ ma?

examples.meaning: Yes, it is. / No, it is not.

u3-location-question.remember: Match the answer to the verb in the question: 在 / 不在 for location, 有 / 沒有 for having, 是 / 不是 for identity. 不在 sounds bú zài before the fourth tone.

u3-all.title: Everyone in the group
u3-all.explanation: 都 means all, or both when the group has two members. It refers to the group before it: 我們都在這裡 means we are all here. Place 都 after that group and before 在 or 是. You can use a counted group too: 兩個學生都在那裡.
u3-all.remember: The order is 我們 + 都 + 在 + 這裡. 都 does not go at the end like too sometimes does in English. Here it is pronounced dōu.

u3-this-person.note: 這 + 個 + 人 is the whole subject: this person. Then use the familiar 是 + identity pattern.

u3-that-person.pinyin: nà ge rén shì wǒ de xuéshēng
u3-that-person.note: 那個人 points to that person. 我的學生 uses the possession pattern from Unit 2.

u3-what-this.note: Keep 什麼 after 是, where the answer will go. It asks for information, so do not add 嗎.

u3-what-that.note: Change 這 to 那 to ask about that. 什麼 stays together as one word.

u3-that-my-book.note: 那 stands alone as that. 我 + 的 + 書 means my book, just like 我的學生 means my student.

u3-one-book.note: 一 (one) + 本 (book measure word) + 書 (book). 一 changes to yì before the third tone of 本.

u3-two-books.note: 兩本書 fills the object slot after 有. Use 兩 before the measure word 本; 書 needs no plural ending.

u3-that-book.note: 那 + 本 + 書 follows the pointing pattern. The measure word changes from 個 to 本 because the noun is book.

u3-big-book.note: 這本書 is the subject. 很 + 大 gives a neutral description here; there is no 是.

u3-small-book.note: Use 小 for small in the same subject + 很 + adjective pattern. 很 need not emphasize very here.

u3-not-big.note: Put 不 directly before 大 for not big. A plain negative description does not need 很 or 是.

u3-im-here.note: 我 (I) + 在 (am at) + 這裡 (here). 在 comes before the place.

u3-book-there.note: The whole phrase 我的書 is the subject. 在 + 那裡 tells you where it is.

u3-is-book-there.pinyin: nǐ de shū zài nàlǐ ma?
u3-is-book-there.note: Add 嗎 to 你的書在那裡. A short answer is 在 or 不在.

u3-all-here.note: 我們 names the group; 都 says all of us. Keep 都 before the verb 在.

u3-all-students.note: 都 refers to everyone in 他們. 是 and 學生 stay the same for a group.

u3-both-there.pinyin: liǎng ge xuéshēng dōu zài nàlǐ
u3-both-there.note: 兩個學生 names a group of two. 都 covers both of them, and 在那裡 gives their location.
